title: New Orleans as a melting pot and ethnic nicknames
summary: Albert says his wife's family includes Filipinos and Chinese, describes the Turks, and explains that nicknames like Turk, Chinese and Dutch were not insults.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, as they say, New Orleans was a melting pot and that's a good name to give it. Because in my wife's family, they're Filipinos, they're Chinamans, and they're various other races. And then, I remember the Turks were here. They were people that were dog-skinned, reddish complexion, with jet black string hair, beautiful. And they're intermarried and if you notice around New Orleans, they can find a lot of these fellow clown hair. But that type of hair, that complexion, they call them a nickname, Turk. Well, that's where they come from, that intermarriage there.

Well, you know, at one time they had a lot of Turkish tunes out, you know, American songs, but with Turkish tones, flavor to them. That's right. And Chinese flavor and all that. And I wondered why. People here liked them. Maybe that had something to do with it?
Well, you still hear people called Turk and Chinese. I hear that Chinese is very common and Dutch, you said, their sister is called Dutch.
They call them that because of their background or their looks, their physical looks.
And then nationally, they do have that part of blood in them that comes from that type of people.
Nobody thought anything about calling anybody anything like that then?
No insults. If it was a little nickname, it wasn't an insulting name.
